newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish police say IRA planned "mass murder".
newsitem.headline: N.Irish police say IRA planned "mass murder".

text.p: Northern Irish police on Thursday accused IRA guerrillas of plotting carnage with a van full of explosives found abandoned near a hotel.

"I have no doubt that the intention of the terrorists was to engage in...nothing else but mass murder of police officers and perhaps soldiers," said Royal Ulster Constabulary superintendent Michael Brown.
Brown, speaking after the bomb was made safe by British army experts, said he believed the outlawed Irish Republican Army had hoped to lure security forces into a trap.

The incident, the latest in a spate of guerrilla hostilites in the British-ruled province, deepened gloom about fraught peace efforts and triggered fears of retaliation by pro-British Loyalist militants.

The IRA, which is fighting to end British sovereignty, telephoned news media on Tuesday night saying they had abandoned a landmine in the van in parkland close to Belfast Castle, an historic former private mansion.
The building, now used as a restaurant and conference centre, was packed with New Year's Eve revellers, including a wedding party, who had to be evacuated.
Brown, speaking to reporters when the RUC put the cache on display to the media, said it consisted of 16 bags of home-made fertiliser explosives and a push-button firing pack.

"This is a densely populated area and also an area where large numbers of teenagers frequent, especially at a time like New Year's Eve. So the potential for death and injury with this device doesn't bear thinking about."
Brown called for vigilance, saying: "Anyone would be extremely foolish not to be concerned about the prospects for the coming weeks."
A leading Loyalist politician Gary McMichael also condemned the IRA for trying to wreck the region's peace efforts.
"This is yet another indication that the IRA is not genuinely interested in building a meaningful peace process," Ulster Democratic Party leader McMichael told Reuters.

"The quantity of the explosives suggests that they were intending to explode a massive bomb and their objective was to cause optimum injury or loss of life. This does not bode well for the possibility of an inclusive peace process."

McMichael, whose party is the political arm of a banned Loyalist guerrilla group, said: "Loyalists are fast coming to the conclusion that we are being driven towards conflict by the IRA....We (UDP) will be doing everthing in our power to ensure that the (Loyalist) ceasefire remains intact."

Anxiety that the region could slide into a cycle of tit-for-tat violence has been fuelled by two recent booby-trap attacks on senior republicans, which media reports have blamed on Loyalists out to avenge IRA hostilities.
Commanders of the Loyalist extremists, so-called because of an unswerving allegiance to British rule, have remained silent about the attacks.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew on Wednesday condemned the attacks but said he did not think that a Loyalist two-year truce had ended.
Britain insists the IRA, fighting to end British rule, must call a ceasefire to win a seat for its Sinn Fein political wing in talks. Sinn Fein wants an unconditional place at the talks.
